np1-chn-basics:
## The big idea
Think of a town with one leaking water pipe. You can keep treating each sick person, or you can fix the pipe. Community health nursing fixes the pipe: the **whole community** is the client, and prevention comes before cure.

## In plain words
- Four kinds of clients, small to big: one person, the **family**, a group with something in common (like school children), and the community.
- The family is the **unit of service**. The community is the **ultimate client**.
- Care is preventive, promotive, curative and rehabilitative, and it keeps going over time.
- Nurses work at home, the health center, clinics, schools and workplaces.

## Easy way to remember
Pick the answer that helps many people and works with them, not just for them.

## Check against your textbook
Names, dates and lists of roles differ between books.
np1-health-promotion:
## The big idea
Health promotion is like training before a race, not fixing an injury after it. It helps people take more control of their health while they are still well or only at risk.

## In plain words
- Promotion builds wellness. **Prevention** avoids one particular disease. That is the main difference.
- Promotion sits in the first (primary) level of prevention, together with things like immunization.
- Good habits to teach: a balanced diet, regular moderate exercise, less salt, sugar and saturated fat, and avoiding tobacco and alcohol.
- Stop exercising and get help if there is chest pain, severe breathlessness or dizziness.

## What the nurse does
First find out if the person is ready to change. Then agree on a small, realistic goal that fits their food, work and budget.

## Common trap
Blood sugar testing is screening, so it is **not** health promotion.

## Check against your textbook
Food-guide models, exercise targets and theory details differ between books.
np1-three-levels-of-prevention:
## The big idea
Picture a fire. Primary prevention stops it from starting. Secondary prevention spots a small fire early and puts it out. Tertiary prevention repairs the damage and helps the house work again.

## In plain words
- **Primary:** before any disease. Healthy living teaching, immunization, handwashing, safe water.
- **Secondary:** find it early and treat it quickly. Screening, a Pap smear, checking blood pressure, testing a coughing contact.
- **Tertiary:** the illness or disability is already there. Limit the damage and rehabilitate, like physical therapy after a stroke.

## How to decide
Look at where the person is **right now**, not at the disease name. Tuberculosis can have all three levels.

## Easy way to remember
Primary = Prevent. Secondary = Seek early. Tertiary = Take care of damage.

## Check against your textbook
Some books split the three levels into five, and group "prompt treatment" differently.
np1-g-phn-roles:
## The big idea
A public health nurse wears many hats at once, like a person who is a teacher, a coordinator and a record-keeper in the same day. Exam questions describe one action and ask which hat it is.

## In plain words
- **Care provider:** looks after the sick at home, clinic, school or work.
- **Educator or trainer:** teaches, counsels and trains midwives.
- **Coordinator:** links people to services.
- **Manager:** makes and carries out the nursing plan.
- **Community organizer:** gets people involved in community work.
- **Change agent:** helps people change a health habit.
- **Role model:** lives a healthy life where others can see it.
- **Recorder:** writes down care and studies the numbers.

## Easy way to match
Nurse tallies cases: recorder. Nurse teaches midwives: trainer. Nurse helps people quit smoking: change agent.

## Check against your textbook
The exact qualification list can change with civil service rules.
np1-mch-program:
## The big idea
This program keeps mothers and children safe from before birth through early childhood. Think of it as a safety net with three parts: care in pregnancy, care after birth, and care of the child.

## In plain words
- **Pregnancy:** register early, go to regular check-ups, take iron and folic acid, and learn the danger signs.
- **Danger signs mean refer right away:** vaginal bleeding, convulsions, severe headache with blurred vision, severe belly pain, leaking fluid.
- **Breastfeeding:** start in the first hour and give only breast milk for six months. Not even water.
- **Sick child (IMCI):** look for general danger signs first. Cannot drink, vomits everything, convulsions, or very sleepy means urgent referral.

## What the nurse does
Danger signs first, then full assessment, treatment, teaching, follow-up.

## Check against your textbook
Visit schedules, supplement timing and breathing-rate cut-offs in this note are doubtful. Check them.
np1-cd-ncd-emergency:
## The big idea
This part of primary health care is the "basic treatment desk" of the health center. It covers common infections, long-term diseases like high blood pressure and diabetes, and emergencies. When a problem is too big, the nurse refers.

## In plain words
- **Communicable diseases** (spread from person to person): follow national protocols, treat dehydration with oral rehydration, finish any medicine course.
- **Noncommunicable diseases** (not spread): heart disease, diabetes, cancer, lung disease. Shared risks you can change: smoking, harmful alcohol, unhealthy food, little exercise.
- **Emergencies:** airway, breathing, circulation first. Call for help early and send a referral note.

## Clinic visit order
Register, wait, triage, evaluation, lab, referral, prescription, health education. Emergency cases skip the line and get first aid.

## Check against your textbook
Protocols, program names and hotline numbers change. Check local policy.
np1-family-assessment:
## The big idea
In community nursing the **family**, not the single patient, is the one being cared for. Assessment is like a home inspection: first look at the whole house, then ask what is stopping the family from fixing its problems.

## In plain words
- **First-level assessment:** who is in the family, their income and beliefs, the home and its water and toilet, each person's health.
- **Second-level assessment:** can the family do its five health jobs? Notice a problem, decide what to do, care for a sick member, keep a healthy home, use community services.
- **Three kinds of problems:**
  - **Threat:** a risk, but no disease yet (unsafe water).
  - **Deficit:** illness or disability already present.
  - **Foreseeable crisis:** a stressful time you can see coming, like childbirth.

## Check against your textbook
Books use slightly different names for the levels, tasks and for wellness potential.
np1-x-chn-process:
## The big idea
This is the usual nursing process (assess, plan, act, evaluate), but the patient is a family or a whole community. Like planning a trip: know where you are, choose a goal, pick the route, travel, then check if you arrived.

## In plain words
- **Assess:** find out how far the group is from the best health it could reach. Findings can be a health deficit, a health threat, a foreseeable crisis or wellness potential.
- **Plan:** set goals first, then choose actions and resources, then set priorities and a schedule. Decide how you will judge success now, not later.
- **Implement:** do the actions and write them down.
- **Evaluate:** check the structure (staff and supplies), the process (how the work was done) and the outcome (did health change).

## Common trap
Documentation belongs to the doing step, not only the end.

## Check against your textbook
Wellness potential is a separate category in some books and not in others.
np1-einc-amtsl:
## The big idea
The first hour of a baby's life has a set order, like a recipe where the steps cannot be swapped. EINC is the recipe for the baby. AMTSL is the recipe for delivering the placenta safely and avoiding heavy bleeding in the mother.

## In plain words
- **EINC for a well baby:** dry right away, place the baby skin-to-skin on mom, clamp the cord late, then breastfeed in the first hour. Eye care, vaccines and weighing wait until after.
- **If the baby is not breathing or crying:** stop the routine and start resuscitation.
- **AMTSL:** a uterus-contracting medicine first, then gentle pulling on the cord while the other hand supports the uterus, then uterine massage.
- Afterward, check the womb is firm and watch the bleeding.

## Common trap
Pulling the cord without supporting the uterus can turn it inside out.

## Check against your textbook
Cord clamping time and timing of vitamin K and vaccines differ by source.
np1-g-hsra-fourmula:
## The big idea
The Department of Health had a big plan to improve the health system, called the Health Sector Reform Agenda. FOURmula One was the action plan for it. Think of a four-legged table: each leg has its own job.

## In plain words
- **Financing:** put in more and steadier money. PhilHealth is the example.
- **Regulation:** keep health goods and services good and affordable.
- **Service delivery:** make sure basic care can be reached.
- **Good governance:** make health offices work better at national and local levels.

## Goals
Better health results, a system that responds to people, and fair payment for care.

## How the exam asks
It names a program and asks which of the four it fits. A PhilHealth question points to financing.

## Check against your textbook
The dates and vision years may be replaced by newer frameworks.
np1-family-implementation-evaluation:
## The big idea
Implementation is doing the family care plan, mostly by visiting the home. Evaluation is checking whether the goals were met. Think of a coach: prepare before the match, play it, then review the score.

## In plain words
- **Before the visit:** read the family record and set a clear goal for the visit.
- **At the visit:** greet, say why you came, observe, wash hands, use the nursing bag carefully, give care and teaching, write it down, set the next appointment.
- **How often to visit:** the family's needs matter most, then whether the family accepts visits. A newborn with a danger sign is visited sooner than a stable family.
- **Evaluation:** was the goal met, partly met, or not met? If not, find out why before repeating the same thing.

## Bag technique in one line
Protect the bag from the home, and protect the family from germs: clean surface, clean hands before and after.

## Check against your textbook
Exact bag steps and forms vary by school and local office.
np1-doh:
## The big idea
The Department of Health is the "rule-maker and coach" of the country's health system. Local governments are the "players" who run most basic services in barangays and towns.

## In plain words
- **DOH jobs:** lead on policy, help others build skills and set quality standards, and run a few special services such as selected national hospitals and emergency response.
- **Local government jobs:** run the health centers and basic services. This shift is called devolution.
- **Referral ladder:** barangay health station, then rural health unit or city health office, then district, provincial and regional hospitals, then national centers.
- **Barangay health workers** are trained community volunteers. The public health nurse supervises midwives and these workers.

## Easy way to decide
Question about national policy or standards: DOH. Question about delivering basic service in a town: local government.

## Common trap
Rural health units belong to the municipality, not the DOH.

## Check against your textbook
Vision years, agency lists and structure change over time.
np1-g-local-health-system:
## The big idea
A law moved the running of health services from the national level down to local governments. Because one town is often too small to run everything alone, towns can team up into a "health zone", like neighbors sharing one bigger clinic network.

## In plain words
- **Devolution:** health staff, buildings and budgets went to local governments.
- **Inter-local health zone:** nearby local governments work together as one system.
- **Four parts of a zone:** people, clear boundaries, health facilities working as one, and the right mix of health workers.

## Why it matters
The public health nurse works for the local government but still follows national health program rules.

## Check against your textbook
The population size for a zone comes from the handout. Confirm it.
np1-incidence-prevalence-pyramid:
## The big idea
Imagine a bathtub. **Incidence** is the water pouring in now (new cases). **Prevalence** is all the water in the tub (everyone who has the disease, old and new).

## In plain words
- **Incidence:** new cases in a time period among people who could still get the disease.
- **Prevalence:** all existing cases at a time or over a period, out of the whole population.
- Better treatment that keeps people alive makes prevalence go up even if no new cases appear.
- **Population pyramid:** a picture of ages and sexes. A wide bottom means many children. A narrow bottom means fewer births and an older population.
- Many children means plan immunization and nutrition. Many older people means plan for long-term diseases.

## Easy way to remember
Incidence = Incoming. Prevalence = Pool.

## Check against your textbook
Formulas and age cut-offs for dependency ratio differ between books.
np1-elements-of-phc:
## The big idea
Primary health care is a basic toolkit of eight services delivered close to home. Students use the word **ELEMENTS**, one letter for each service, to remember them.

## In plain words
- **E**ducation for health
- **L**ocally endemic disease control
- **E**xpanded Program on Immunization
- **M**aternal and child health, with family planning
- **E**ssential drugs
- **N**utrition
- **T**reatment of common illnesses and injuries
- **S**anitation

## Four pillars that hold it up
Community participation, working with other sectors, appropriate technology (simple tools people can afford and keep up), and support systems. Participation is asked most often.

## Easy way to match
Ask what the main purpose of the activity is. A latrine is sanitation. Weighing preschoolers is nutrition.

## Check against your textbook
Books word the letters differently, and some add mental health or oral health.
np1-phc-basics:
## The big idea
Primary health care means health services that are close to home, affordable, acceptable and built with the people. It is both the first place people get care and a way of thinking: health for everyone, not only those who can reach a hospital.

## In plain words
- International push: the Alma-Ata Declaration in 1978. Philippine adoption: LOI 949 in 1979.
- It includes promotive, preventive, curative and rehabilitative care.
- It works with other fields like education, agriculture and housing, because health depends on more than medicine.
- Workers: barangay health workers and volunteers, plus the public health nurse, midwife and rural doctor.

## How to choose answers
Prefer community-based over hospital-based, prevention over cure, and simple technology over fancy machines.

## Easy way to remember
Four A's: Accessible, Acceptable, Affordable, Appropriate.

## Check against your textbook
The Philippine date and theme year come from the handout. Verify them.
np1-x-subspecialties:
## The big idea
Three phrases sound alike but mean different things. Think of them as three different jobs in the same neighborhood.

## In plain words
- **Community health nursing:** nursing plus public health, aimed at keeping whole populations healthy.
- **Community-based nursing:** care of individuals and families as they move among services outside the hospital, such as a patient followed at home after discharge.
- **Public health nursing:** nursing, public health and some social help working together for the whole population.
- Clients come in four levels: individual, family, population, community.
- **Subspecialties:** school nursing, occupational (workplace) health nursing, community mental health nursing, public health nursing.

## Easy way to match
Nurse in a factory watching worker hazards: occupational health. Nurse screening pupils: school nursing.

## Common trap
Community-based and public health nursing are not the same thing.

## Check against your textbook
Attributions and wording come from the handout. Verify them.
np1-phc-elements:
## The big idea
This is the same list of eight primary health care services, with a focus on matching real-life activities to the right service. The word **ELEMENTS** helps you remember them.

## In plain words
- Teaching handwashing: education.
- Dengue or malaria case finding: locally endemic disease control.
- BCG, measles and pentavalent shots: immunization.
- Prenatal visits and birth spacing: maternal and child health, with family planning.
- Generic drugs and herbal plants: essential drugs.
- Vitamin A, iron and breastfeeding: nutrition.
- First aid and care for high blood pressure: treatment.
- Toilets and safe water: sanitation.

## What the nurse does
Teach at every contact, because every other service depends on people understanding it. Then focus on what local data shows is the biggest gap.

## Common trap
Emergency care is not "essential drugs".

## Check against your textbook
Exact names, order and wording of the treatment element vary.
np1-endemic-diseases:
## The big idea
"Endemic" means a disease that is always present in an area, like a house that always has a few mosquitoes. To control these diseases, learn how each one travels and break the link.

## In plain words
- **Tuberculosis:** spreads through the air. Treated for six months under direct observation so the person does not skip doses. Rifampicin can turn urine orange, which is expected.
- **Dengue:** daytime Aedes mosquito in clean standing water. Most danger comes after the fever drops. No aspirin.
- **Malaria:** night-biting Anopheles mosquito. Use nets and treat early.
- **Schistosomiasis:** from snails in water that touches the skin.
- **Filariasis:** mosquito bite, can cause swollen limbs years later.
- **Leprosy:** slow skin and nerve disease. Early patches lose feeling.
- **Rabies:** from the saliva of an infected animal. Wash a bite wound at once and seek care.

## What the nurse does
Treat urgent signs first, then report cases and clean up the surroundings.

## Check against your textbook
Treatments, drugs and which diseases count as endemic change by place. Check local policy.
np1-epidemiology-endemic:
## The big idea
This is a signpost note. It points you to the detailed notes on disease patterns and on common local diseases. Epidemiology means studying who gets sick, where and why, so you can stop the spread.

## In plain words
- **Sporadic:** a few scattered cases.
- **Endemic:** the usual level in a place.
- **Epidemic:** unusually many cases in a short time.
- **Pandemic:** spread across several countries.
- Control is easiest at the link where the germ travels, the mode of transmission.

## What the nurse does
Treat urgent cases first, then report and look at local numbers to find the biggest problem.

## Common trap
An epidemic is judged against what is normal for that place, not by raw numbers alone.

## Check against your textbook
Which diseases your book calls endemic, and the named areas, can differ.
np1-epi-overview:
## The big idea
Vaccines work best when most people in a community have them. Then the germ has nowhere to spread, and even people who cannot be vaccinated are protected. This is called herd immunity. The Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) is the national plan to make that happen.

## In plain words
- Safe to give all EPI vaccines on the same day at different body sites.
- If a dose is missed, just give it later. Do not restart the series.
- Mild illness, a cold, low fever, diarrhea or malnutrition are **not** reasons to skip a vaccine.
- Real reasons to hold back: for example, a child who had convulsions or shock within 3 days of the last DPT dose, or a weak immune system for live vaccines.
- One needle and one syringe per child.
- Chikiting Ligtas is the name for mass catch-up campaigns.

## What the nurse does
Check the vaccine card, screen for real reasons to wait, give the right vaccine correctly, record it, and follow up children who missed doses.

## Check against your textbook
The schedule has changed since the handout. Check current ages, vaccines and law numbers.
np1-family-planning:
## The big idea
A family usually has many problems but the nurse has little time. Planning means picking which problem to work on first, setting goals, and deciding who does what. It is like choosing which leak to fix first in a house.

## In plain words
- A **goal** is the big purpose. **Objectives** are small, clear, measurable steps.
- The family helps set the goals so they will accept them.
- A scoring scale ranks problems using four criteria: nature of the problem, preventive potential, modifiability (can it be changed?) and salience (does the family see it as urgent?).
- Modifiability counts double because effort only pays off if the problem can really change.
- Add up the scores. The highest total goes first.

## Safety rule
A life-threatening or fast-spreading problem comes first, whatever the score says.

## Common trap
Forgetting to multiply by the weight.

## Check against your textbook
The exact scores and weights are not from the handout. Copy your school's version.
np1-g-fp-permanent-hormonal:
## The big idea
Family planning helps couples choose how many children to have and when. Methods range from permanent to temporary. The nurse counsels, provides services and keeps supplies available.

## In plain words
- **Tubal ligation (female) and vasectomy (male):** permanent, hard to reverse. They do not protect against infections spread by sex.
- **Pill:** needs steady daily use and may reduce breast milk.
- **Injectable:** a hormone shot that is reversible and needs no daily action.
- **Condom:** the one listed here that also protects against sexually transmitted infections.
- **LAM (breastfeeding method):** temporary, works for up to six months, and needs full breastfeeding.

## How the exam asks
Which method protects against infections? Condom. Which can reduce lactation? Pill. LAM lasts how long? Six months.

## Check against your textbook
Rules for who may use which method, such as combined pills while breastfeeding, vary. Confirm them.
np1-phc-pillars-characteristics:
## The big idea
Primary health care stands on four supports, like four legs of a chair. If one is weak, the program wobbles.

## In plain words
- **Community participation:** the people take part in decisions and actions. This comes first because ownership keeps programs alive.
- **Linkages:** working with other groups, such as schools, local government and other fields, not only the health office.
- **Appropriate technology:** simple, affordable and fitting local culture.
- **Support mechanisms:** money, trained people and supplies to keep services going.

## Easy way to match
Villagers decide: participation. Health center teams up with a school: linkage. Simple, locally made: appropriate technology. Budget and trained staff: support.

## Easy way to remember
P-I-T-S: Participation, Intersectoral, Technology, Support.

## Common trap
An expensive machine is not appropriate technology.

## Check against your textbook
Some schools teach three pillars instead of four.
np1-g-levels-care-referral:
## The big idea
Health care is like stairs with three steps. You start at the lowest step close to home, and you are sent up only when the problem needs more skill or equipment. A good referral system also lets you come back down for follow-up.

## In plain words
- **Primary level:** first contact. Barangay health station, rural health unit, health center. Staffed by nurses, midwives, community health workers.
- **Secondary level:** doctors with basic training, minor surgery, simple lab tests. District or provincial hospitals.
- **Tertiary level:** specialists, complicated cases, intensive care. Regional and national medical centers.

## What the nurse does
Keep simple cases at the primary level. In an emergency referral, accompany the client.

## Check against your textbook
Some sources place a community hospital at the secondary level instead of primary.
np1-levels-of-prevention:
## The big idea
Prevention has three timings: before disease, while it is starting, and after damage is done. Questions give an action and ask which timing it is. Ask: has the disease already happened?

## In plain words
- **Primary:** not sick yet. Teaching healthy habits, immunization, safe water, handwashing, prenatal care.
- **Secondary:** find it early and treat quickly. Screening tests, breast self-examination, sputum test, noticing cancer warning signs.
- **Tertiary:** damage or disability already there. Rehabilitation, crutch walking, physical therapy.
- One disease can use all three levels. Diabetes: healthy diet to prevent it, screening to catch it, foot and eye care to prevent complications.

## Common traps
Screening is secondary, not primary. Breast self-examination is done at home but it looks for disease, so it is secondary.

## Easy way to remember
Prevent it, catch it, limit it.

## Check against your textbook
Some books treat promotion as its own level or add another level. Follow your school.
np1-g-clinic-visit:
## The big idea
A visit to the health center follows a set path, like a line at a counter. Everyone follows the same order, except real emergencies, who go first.

## In plain words
1. **Registration:** greet the client, open or find the family record, note the complaint and history.
2. **Waiting:** priority numbers, first come first served.
3. **Triage:** sorting by urgency. Program cases follow protocol, other cases go to the doctor, emergencies get first aid.
4. **Clinical evaluation:** check the history and exam, decide on treatment, explain it.
5. **Laboratory:** send to the referral lab if needed.
6. **Referral:** two-way. Go along with the client in an emergency.
7. **Medicine:** give or prescribe, and teach how to take it.
8. **Health education:** one-on-one counseling and the next appointment.

## Why emergencies skip the line
Safety and airway, breathing and circulation come first.

## Check against your textbook
The exact steps and wording can differ by health center and local policy.
np1-g-management-functions:
## The big idea
Managing a health program is like running a trip. You decide where to go, arrange the team, tell them the plan, keep everyone in step, watch for wandering off course, and finally judge how it went.

## In plain words
- **Planning:** decide what needs to be done.
- **Organizing:** decide how, and who has which job.
- **Directing:** tell workers the plan.
- **Coordinating:** link the team members.
- **Controlling:** check work against standards and correct drift.
- **Evaluating:** judge whether the program worked.

## Easy way to match
Writing job descriptions: organizing. Checking staff output against standards: controlling. Holding a meeting to explain the plan: directing.

## Common trap
Controlling corrects during the work. Evaluating judges the results.

## Check against your textbook
Some books list only four or five functions.
np1-competency-based-teaching:
## The big idea
Teaching is not finished when you finish talking. It is finished when the learner can really do the thing. Competency-based teaching starts with what the learner must be able to do and then checks it.

## In plain words
- Three kinds of learning: **knowing** (cognitive), **attitude** (affective) and **doing** (psychomotor).
- Match the method: talks and discussion for knowing, role play for attitude, demonstration and return demonstration for doing.
- Return demonstration means the learner performs the skill while you watch.
- Adults learn best when the topic is useful to them now.

## What the nurse does
Assess what the learner already knows and believes. Set a clear goal. Teach in small steps. Check by watching them do it, and reteach if needed.

## Common trap
A lecture or a written test cannot prove a hands-on skill.

## Check against your textbook
This note is general teaching principles. Your school may use different terms.
np1-health-education:
## The big idea
Health education is the first of the eight primary health care services. The goal is that people can really do healthy things, not just repeat facts. Good teaching starts with the learner.

## In plain words
- Learning has three parts: knowing, feeling or valuing, and doing.
- **Teach-back:** the learner explains it back in their own words.
- **Return demonstration:** the learner shows the skill while you watch.
- Teach simple things before complex ones, and known things before new ones.
- Demonstrations and personal contact change behavior more than mass media does.
- Words in goals give clues. "Demonstrate" means doing. "Explain" means knowing. "Express willingness" means attitude.

## What the nurse does
Check readiness and language first. If the client is in pain or in an emergency, treat that first and teach later.

## Common trap
Attendance or "the client said yes" does not prove learning. Shown behavior does.

## Check against your textbook
Teaching models and verb lists differ between schools.
np1-g-bp-technique:
## The big idea
Taking blood pressure the same careful way each time gives readings you can trust. Exams like to ask about small mistakes in the steps.

## In plain words
- Before: client rested 5 minutes, no smoking or caffeine in the previous 30 minutes.
- Bare the arm. Cuff snug with no creases above the elbow crease. Arm supported at heart level, gauge at eye level.
- **Palpate first:** find the pulse, inflate until it disappears, note that number, release fully and wait a minute or two.
- **Then listen:** stethoscope over the brachial pulse, inflate above the first number, release slowly.
- The first clear tapping sound is the top number. When the sound disappears, that is the bottom number.
- Record the average of two readings taken a couple of minutes apart.

## Check against your textbook
Books differ on bell versus diaphragm of the stethoscope. Confirm which your school teaches.
np1-g-home-visit-bag:
## The big idea
A home visit is a planned professional visit to see the family where they live. The nursing bag is a small portable toolkit, packed so that germs do not travel between homes.

## In plain words
- Every visit needs a purpose and a plan, and the family should be involved.
- Reasons to visit: give care, check living conditions, teach prevention, link to services.
- Steps: greet, say why you came, observe, set the bag down in a convenient clean place, give care and teaching, write it down, set the next visit.
- How often to visit depends first on the family's needs, second on how well they accept visits.
- Keep the bag clean, stocked with supplies and emergency items, and protected from touching other things.

## Check against your textbook
Exact bag steps and contents can vary by agency or home.
np1-epidemiology-fhsis:
## The big idea
Epidemiology asks who gets sick, where, when and why, and then uses the answers to control disease. FHSIS is the paper system where health centers record their work and send the numbers upward.

## In plain words
- Disease often has several causes acting together. The triad: agent (the germ), host (the person), environment.
- Four approaches: describe (who, where, when), analyze (why), test a new control method, and evaluate programs.
- Surveillance means collecting and using data on a steady basis.
- **FHSIS pieces:** the Family Treatment Record (building block), the Target Client List (tracks eligible clients), reporting forms (move data upward), output reports.
- Patterns: sporadic, endemic, epidemic, pandemic.

## What the nurse does
Record every contact on time. Report notifiable diseases quickly. In an outbreak, start control while the investigation goes on.

## Check against your textbook
Current form names, reporting schedules and any electronic version may differ.
np1-vital-statistics:
## The big idea
Vital statistics count births, illnesses and deaths so you can see how healthy a community is and whether health work is helping. Think of them as a community report card.

## In plain words
- A **rate** has a top number (events), a bottom number (the group at risk) and a multiplier such as per 1,000.
- **Birth rate** and **death rate** use the midyear population.
- **Infant mortality:** infant deaths over live births. A good sign of a community's general health.
- **Maternal mortality:** deaths linked to pregnancy and birth over live births. It reflects the quality of obstetric care.
- **Case fatality:** deaths from a disease over cases of that disease.
- **Attack rate:** new cases in an outbreak among those exposed.

## How to solve a problem
Find the right bottom number first, then multiply.

## Easy way to remember
Swaroop's index: old deaths over all deaths.

## Check against your textbook
Multipliers and rate-versus-ratio wording differ between books.
np1-x-epi-concepts:
## The big idea
Epidemiology is detective work for whole populations: who is getting sick, where, when, and why. Then you try something to stop it and check if it worked.

## In plain words
- **Multiple causation:** diseases usually have several causes working together, not just one.
- **Natural history of disease:** first a "before the germ acts" stage, then three stages: no symptoms yet, visible changes, advanced disease.
- **Four approaches, in order:**
  - **Descriptive:** count cases by person, place and time.
  - **Analytical:** test why it happens.
  - **Experimental:** try a new way of controlling it.
  - **Evaluation:** judge whether services and programs work.

## Easy way to match
Counts and rates by place and time: descriptive. Trying a new bednet: experimental. Judging a program's results: evaluation.

## Common trap
Do not confuse experimental with evaluation.

## Check against your textbook
Some books name only three approaches.
np1-x-fhsis-blocks:
## The big idea
FHSIS is a layered record system, like building a wall brick by brick. Each layer is made from the layer below, so a mistake at the bottom spreads upward.

## In plain words
- **Family Treatment Record:** the first and most basic building block. One record per family member, filled in at each contact.
- **Target Client List:** the second block. A list of eligible clients for a program, such as all pregnant women, showing what they still need.
- **Reporting forms:** the only route data takes from one facility to another, monthly or quarterly.
- **Output reports:** made so managers can use the results.

## What the nurse does
Record at the time of service. Keep the client list updated so missed or due clients can be found.

## Common trap
Do not swap the first and second building blocks.

## Check against your textbook
Current forms and any electronic versions may differ.
np1-g-maternal-prenatal-supplements:
## The big idea
This is the standard care package for a mother from early pregnancy to after birth. Think of it as a checklist of visits, supplements and teaching.

## In plain words
- **Visits:** first as early as possible, then once in the second trimester, once in the third, and every two weeks after the eighth month.
- **Supplements:** vitamin A, then iron with folic acid. The handout gives amounts and timing, but they are doubtful.
- **Also in the package:** treatment of problems, clean and safe delivery, birth registration, breastfeeding help, newborn screening and family planning counseling.
- **After birth:** first visit in the first week, second visit at six weeks.
- Space births 3 to 5 years apart.

## Check against your textbook
Vitamin A in pregnancy depends heavily on the source and high doses can harm. Verify the amount and timing with current DOH guidance before using it.
np1-newborn-screening:
## The big idea
A few drops of blood from a baby's heel can reveal rare but treatable conditions before they cause damage. A normal-looking baby can still have one. Screening is a first alert, not a diagnosis.

## In plain words
- The test checks for conditions such as an underactive thyroid, milk-sugar problems, protein-processing problems and G6PD deficiency. Untreated, they can cause intellectual disability, poor growth or death.
- A positive screen means "needs a confirming test and fast treatment".
- Timing matters. Too early can miss problems.

## What the nurse does
Explain the test to parents. Warm the foot and use the side of the heel. Fill each circle fully from one side, let the card dry flat away from heat and sun, and send it quickly. Follow up positive results at once.

## Common trap
A wet, smeared or layered card is rejected and the test repeated.

## Check against your textbook
The timing window and the list of conditions differ between sources and have expanded.
np1-nutrition:
## The big idea
Malnutrition is not only too little food. It can also be too much, or the wrong nutrients. Children who are malnourished get infections more easily and grow poorly.

## In plain words
- **Marasmus:** a very thin, wasted child who looks hungry, with no swelling.
- **Kwashiorkor:** swollen feet, face and belly because of low protein. "Swollen" is kwashiorkor, "wasted" is marasmus.
- **Vitamin A lack:** night blindness and dry eyes.
- **Iron lack:** anemia, which means pallor and tiredness.
- **Iodine lack:** goiter. Iodized salt protects.
- Rice, flour, edible oil and sugar must be fortified by law.
- Breastfeed in the first hour, give only breast milk for six months, add foods at six months, continue to two years.

## What the nurse does
Look for danger signs first and refer if present. Measure, classify, supplement and teach.

## Check against your textbook
Schedules, law numbers and cut-offs change. Older advice about AIDS and breastfeeding may differ today.
np1-g-fp-natural:
## The big idea
Natural family planning means finding the days a woman can get pregnant, then avoiding sex or using a barrier on those days. It only works when both partners cooperate.

## In plain words
- **Mucus (Billings) method:** watch cervical mucus.
- **Basal body temperature:** take temperature daily and watch for the rise after ovulation.
- **Sympto-thermal:** combines mucus, temperature and other signs.
- **Two-day method:** any secretions today or yesterday mean fertile days.
- **Standard days method:** colored cycle beads mark fertile and infertile days. For women whose cycles are usually 26 to 32 days.

## Cautions
Unusual discharge makes mucus methods unreliable. Not advised if pregnancy would be dangerous.

## Check against your textbook
The handout wording on the standard days method is reversed. It is meant for women whose cycles are usually 26 to 32 days long.
np1-cold-chain:
## The big idea
Vaccines are fragile, like ice cream and eggs. If they get too warm or freeze when they should not, they stop working without looking different. The cold chain keeps them at the right temperature from maker to child.

## In plain words
- Keep vaccines in the refrigerator, not in the door and not against the cooling plate. Nothing else, such as food, goes in.
- Write down the temperature morning and afternoon.
- **Vaccine vial monitor:** a small square that darkens with heat. If it matches or is darker than the circle, throw the vaccine away.
- **Shake test:** shows whether a vaccine was frozen.
- Use the vial that expires first.
- Light can damage BCG and measles vaccine.

## If power fails
Keep the door closed. Move vaccines to cold boxes with frozen ice packs if the outage continues.

## Common trap
The vial monitor shows heat damage. The shake test shows freezing damage.

## Check against your textbook
Temperature ranges and open-vial rules vary. Verify local policy.
np1-g-iycf:
## The big idea
Infant and young child feeding gives babies the best start and lowers child deaths. The rules for feeding are simple and ordered by age.

## In plain words
- Start breastfeeding in the first hour after birth.
- For six months give **only** breast milk. Not even water.
- At six months add suitable foods that are timely, adequate and safe.
- Keep breastfeeding to two years and beyond.
- Early skin-to-skin contact and early feeding help survival.

## What the nurse does
Teach feeding messages before the mother goes home.

## Check against your textbook
Advice for mothers with HIV has changed over time. Verify current DOH policy.
np1-x-child-health-programs:
## The big idea
This is the list of services for children from birth to 9 years. Think of it as a menu: match the child's need to the right program.

## In plain words
The programs are:
- feeding of infants and young children
- newborn screening
- immunization
- management of childhood illnesses
- micronutrient supplements
- dental health
- early child development
- prevention of child injuries

## What the nurse does
At every contact look for danger signs first. Then give whatever is due, such as a vaccine, vitamin A or feeding advice. Teach caregivers and follow up.

## Common trap
Newborn screening is not part of immunization.

## Check against your textbook
The target year in the handout is outdated. Find the current target.
np1-g-feeding-laws:
## The big idea
Some laws protect breastfeeding and make staple foods more nutritious. The exam wants you to match each law to its topic.

## In plain words
- **Milk Code (EO 51):** controls the marketing of formula and other breast milk substitutes.
- **Rooming-In and Breastfeeding Act (RA 7600):** mother and baby stay together 24 hours.
- **Food Fortification Law (RA 8976):** rice, flour, cooking oil and sugar must be fortified. Processed foods are optional.
- **Expanded Breastfeeding Promotion Act (RA 10028):** supports exclusive breastfeeding for six months.

## Easy way to match
Rooming-in is 7600. Fortification is 8976. Formula marketing is EO 51.

## Check against your textbook
The handout dates RA 10028 differently from other sources. Verify.
np1-x-epi-law-contraindications:
## The big idea
Most mild sicknesses are **not** good reasons to skip a vaccine. Sending a child away for a cold means a missed chance to protect them. Only a few real reasons exist to hold back.

## In plain words
- **Vaccinate anyway:** malnutrition, low-grade fever, mild respiratory infection, cough, diarrhea, vomiting.
- **Real reasons to hold back:** convulsions or shock within 3 days after the last DPT dose; whole-cell pertussis vaccine in a child with neurologic disease; live vaccines such as BCG in someone with a weak immune system from cancer.
- Missed a dose? Just give it. Do not restart, and do not give extra doses.
- Do not give doses closer together than the minimum gap.
- Mix freeze-dried vaccines only with their own diluent. One needle and syringe per child.

## Check against your textbook
Law numbers, protection percentages and the contraindication list should be double-checked.
np1-x-epi-schedule-table:
## The big idea
This is the handout's vaccine timetable. Think of it as a calendar: birth, six weeks, then repeated doses, then nine months.

## In plain words
- At birth: BCG and hepatitis B.
- From 6 weeks: pentavalent and oral polio, three doses each, four weeks apart.
- 9 months: measles.
- 12 months: MMR.
- IPV at 14 weeks.
- BCG goes into the skin. Measles goes just under the skin of the upper arm. Infant muscle shots go into the outer thigh because it has the biggest muscle.
- A child with no vaccines yet can safely get several due vaccines on one day at different body sites.

## Common trap
Measles is not given into the muscle and BCG is not given under the skin.

## Check against your textbook
The Philippine schedule keeps changing. Verify the current one with your instructor.
np1-vaccine-principles:
## The big idea
Every vaccine follows the same safety rules, even though each has its own route and site. Screen first, give carefully, watch afterward.

## In plain words
- **Live vaccines** (BCG, measles, MMR, oral polio, rotavirus) use weakened germs. Avoid them in people with very weak immune systems and in pregnancy.
- **Inactivated vaccines and toxoids** cannot cause the disease but need more doses.
- Never mix vaccines in one syringe. New needle and syringe for each child, and throw sharps away without recapping.
- Mild reactions: sore arm, redness, low fever, irritability.
- A serious allergic reaction is rare but is an emergency. Keep the airway open and get help.
- An abscess at the injection site usually points to unclean technique, not the vaccine.

## Types of immunity
Natural or artificial, active or passive.

## Check against your textbook
The current schedule, observation time after shots and the reporting route should be verified.
np1-bcg-pentavalent:
## The big idea
BCG helps protect small children from the severe forms of tuberculosis. Pentavalent is one shot with five protections in it (penta means five).

## In plain words
- **BCG:** given into the skin at birth. A small raised bump forms right away. That means it went into the right layer.
- A small ulcer and then a scar after some weeks are normal. No ointment, dressing or antibiotics needed.
- **Pentavalent:** goes into the muscle of the baby's outer thigh, three doses starting at 6 weeks.
- It protects against diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, hepatitis B and Hib.
- Mild fever and soreness are common.

## What the nurse does
Screen first. Do not massage the BCG site. Teach warning signs such as spreading redness, high fever or a convulsion.

## Common trap
BCG goes into the skin. Pentavalent goes into the muscle.

## Check against your textbook
Doses, ages and the current pentavalent schedule differ between sources.
np1-g-oral-health:
## The big idea
The oral health program tries to prevent tooth decay and gum disease. Prevent first, treat what is already there.

## In plain words
- **Promote:** teach about brushing and diet.
- **Prevent:** mouth exams, good oral hygiene, sealants on grooves of teeth, fluoride use.
- **Treat:** fillings, gum treatment, pulling a tooth when needed, draining an abscess.
- Pregnant women and older people are named targets for improved oral health.

## What the nurse does
Check teeth and gums, teach brushing and diet, and refer for sealants, fillings or extractions.

## Easy way to decide
Early decay without pain: prevention. An abscess: treatment and referral.

## Check against your textbook
The percentage targets and the 2010 deadline in the handout are old. Look up current goals.
np1-reproductive-health-fp:
## The big idea
Reproductive health means well-being in body, mind and social life in everything to do with reproduction. Family planning is one part. The couple chooses, with full information. The nurse never picks the method for them.

## In plain words
- **Tubal ligation and vasectomy:** permanent. A man needs another method for about 3 months after a vasectomy.
- **Pill:** daily, and may reduce breast milk.
- **Injectable:** a progestin shot, no daily action.
- **Condom:** the only method listed that also blocks infections.
- **IUD:** put in by a trained provider. Teach the string check.
- **LAM:** works only if the baby is under six months, the mother is fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, and her periods have not returned.
- **Natural methods:** mucus, temperature, counting days. They need abstinence on fertile days.

## What the nurse does
Assess first, give full information, let the client choose, teach correct use, follow up.

## Check against your textbook
Which methods the DOH provides now, and the handout wording on the standard days method, which is reversed.
np1-x-reproductive-health-program:
## The big idea
The national reproductive health program has one broad aim, better quality of life, and a list of services it covers. Think of it as a menu of services around reproduction.

## In plain words
Main aims:
- fewer deaths of mothers and children
- stop and reverse the spread of HIV/AIDS
- wider access to information and services

Services include family planning, maternal and child care and nutrition, infections of the reproductive tract, teen reproductive health, complications of abortion, breast and reproductive cancers, sexuality counseling, men's involvement, violence against women and children, and infertility.

## What the nurse does
Assess the need, counsel, refer for what the facility cannot offer, and protect from violence. Safety and life threats come first.

## How the exam asks
Match a described service to its element.

## Check against your textbook
Lists of elements differ between sources.
np1-vawc:
## The big idea
VAWC means violence against women and their children. The law covers abuse by a husband, former partner or someone the woman has or had a relationship with. The nurse's first job is to treat injuries and make sure she is safe, before any legal steps.

## In plain words
- Abuse can be physical, sexual, emotional or economic (controlling money).
- Warning signs: repeated injuries, injuries at different healing stages, fearful behavior, a story that does not fit, a partner who will not leave her side.
- **Protection orders:** the barangay can issue a quick one. The court can issue longer ones.
- A common pattern: tension builds, violence happens, a "honeymoon" phase, then it repeats.

## What the nurse does
Interview her alone in a private, calm place. Believe her. Document with her own words. Refer to the women and children protection unit. Help make a safety plan.

## Common traps
Do not confront the abuser, and do not pressure her to leave or press charges at once.

## Check against your textbook
Law numbers and procedures come from general teaching. Verify.
np1-environmental-sanitation:
## The big idea
Sanitation means making the surroundings safe: clean water, proper toilets, waste handling, safe food and control of pests. Dirty surroundings cause diarrhea, typhoid, hepatitis A, worms and diseases carried by insects. This is a signpost note that points to the detailed ones.

## In plain words
- Sanitation is primary prevention.
- Laws to match:
  - PD 856: Sanitation Code
  - RA 6969: toxic and hazardous waste
  - RA 8749: Clean Air
  - RA 9003: solid waste
  - RA 9275: Clean Water

## What the nurse does
Check the household's water, toilet, waste and food handling. Fix the riskiest exposure first, such as unsafe drinking water or open defecation. Teach, and work with the sanitary inspector.

## Quick fix and lasting fix
Boiling or chlorinating water is the quick fix. Building a toilet is the lasting fix.

## Check against your textbook
Local standards and law numbers should be verified.
np1-water-toilet:
## The big idea
Safe water and proper toilets are the strongest shields against diarrhea and similar diseases. Both use "Level I, II, III", but the two scales are separate, so keep them apart.

## In plain words
**Water**
- **Level I:** a protected well or spring. Source only, no pipes.
- **Level II:** a shared tap, communal faucets.
- **Level III:** a pipe into each house.

**Toilets**
- **Level I:** pit latrine, pour-flush toilet.
- **Level II:** water-carriage toilet with a septic tank.
- **Level III:** water-carriage toilet connected to a septic or sewer system.

## Easy way to remember
Water levels: I at the source, II at a shared tap, III inside the home.

## What the nurse does
Check where drinking water comes from and how it is stored. Boil or chlorinate drinking water as the quick fix, then promote a sanitary toilet. Teach handwashing with soap.

## Common trap
A flushing toilet near a shallow well can still contaminate it.

## Check against your textbook
Household counts, distances and boiling times differ by source.
np1-x-environmental-health-laws:
## The big idea
Environmental health is about preventing illness by managing the surroundings and changing behavior so people are less exposed to harmful agents. Each environmental law covers one kind of hazard.

## In plain words
- **PD 856:** Sanitation Code of the Philippines.
- **RA 6969:** toxic substances and hazardous and nuclear waste.
- **RA 8749:** Clean Air Act.
- **RA 9003:** ecological solid waste management.
- **RA 9275:** Clean Water Act.

## How to match
Look at the hazard in the question (water, air, waste, toxic) and pick the law that covers it.

## What the nurse does
Check hazards in homes and the community. Reduce the most dangerous one first. Teach, work with the sanitary inspector, and report violations and outbreaks.

## Common trap
Do not mix up RA 9003 (everyday solid waste) with RA 6969 (toxic and hazardous waste).

## Check against your textbook
Law numbers and years should be verified.
np1-waste-food-laws:
## The big idea
Keeping a community healthy includes sorting waste properly, handling food safely, and knowing which law covers what.

## In plain words
- **Waste:** sort at the source into food scraps, recyclables, residual and hazardous. Sharps go into puncture-resistant containers.
- **Food safety has four "rights":** right source, right preparation, right cooking, right storage.
  - Keep raw and cooked food apart.
  - Cook food through.
  - Do not leave cooked food out for more than two hours.
- Food handlers need health certificates and should stay away from food when sick.
- When in doubt, throw it out.
- Laws: PD 856 sanitation, RA 9003 solid waste, RA 9275 water, RA 8749 air, RA 6969 toxic waste.

## What the nurse does
Inspect hazards, protect people first, teach segregation, handwashing and safe cooking, and report outbreaks.

## Check against your textbook
Bin color codes, holding temperatures and certificate rules should be verified locally.
np1-x-water-toilet-specs:
## The big idea
The handout gives the numbers behind each level of water and toilet facility. These are fact-recall items, so link each number to a picture.

## In plain words
- **Water Level I:** protected well or spring, serves about 15 to 25 households, farthest user within 250 meters.
- **Water Level II:** communal faucet, within 25 meters of the farthest house, about one faucet for every 4 to 6 households.
- **Water Level III:** house connections.
- Open dug wells and unimproved springs are not approved.
- Disinfect any new or repaired water source.
- **Toilet levels:** I no-flush or low-water, II water-carriage with a septic tank, III connected to a sewer system.

## What the nurse does
Classify the facility, disinfect and test questionable water, and teach handwashing.

## Common trap
Do not swap 250 meters (Level I) with 25 meters (Level II).

## Check against your textbook
Household counts and distances differ among sources.
np1-x-food-safety:
## The big idea
Safe food follows four simple rules, like a short checklist: Source, Preparation, Cooking, Storage. Food places are also inspected and rated.

## In plain words
- **Right source:** buy fresh food, check expiry dates, avoid dented or bulging cans.
- **Right preparation:** keep raw and cooked foods apart, wash raw vegetables, wash hands and utensils.
- **Right cooking:** cook all parts through and eat promptly.
- **Right storage:** cooked food no more than two hours at room temperature, in tight containers. Reheat well.
- When in doubt, throw it out.
- Food establishments are rated Class A (excellent), B (very satisfactory) or C (satisfactory).
- Food handlers need health certificates.

## What the nurse does
Find the likely food source and stop further exposure first. Check handlers' health. Teach the four rights.

## Common trap
Do not confuse the two-hour storage rule with the cooking temperature.

## Check against your textbook
Temperatures and hours come from the handout. Verify locally.
np1-sentrong-sigla:
## The big idea
Sentrong Sigla is a quality seal for health centers, like a restaurant star rating. The DOH checks whether a center meets set standards. Meeting them earns recognition.

## In plain words
- It is about **quality**, not money. It is not PhilHealth.
- Three steps up: Basic certification, then Specialty Awards, then Awards for Excellence.
- Excellence needs high standards kept for at least three years in a row.
- Certification lasts two years.
- A center that slips back keeps the seal but does not get the renewal sticker.

## What the nurse does
Know the standards, keep records and equipment ready for checking, and keep improving after getting the seal.

## Common trap
A facility that slips back does not lose the seal at once.

## Check against your textbook
The standards, levels and even the program's present name may have changed. Verify.
np1-essential-drugs-herbal:
## The big idea
Essential drugs are medicines that most people need and should be able to afford. Generic medicines cost less than brands with the same ingredient. Some tested herbal plants are also endorsed as lower-cost options. Herbal remedies support proven treatment, they do not replace it.

## In plain words
- **Generic** means the medicine is sold by its chemical name.
- **Botika ng Barangay:** a community drugstore in a far-away barangay, run by a community group with a licensed pharmacist supervising.
- Herb safety rules: use the right plant and the right part, one plant at a time, stop if there is a reaction, and see a doctor if there is no improvement after two or three doses.
- Boil in clay or enamel pots, not aluminum. Avoid plants sprayed with insecticide.
- Common matches: lagundi for cough, sambong for swelling, akapulko for skin infections, ampalaya for blood sugar, niyog-niyogan for roundworm.

## Check against your textbook
The official herb list, plant parts and preparation amounts should be verified before teaching.
np1-g-herbal-guidelines:
## The big idea
Herbal plants can help, but they are still medicine. The rules are simple safety habits, like checking a recipe before you cook.

## In plain words
- Use the right plant, the right part, and the recommended amount.
- Use **one** plant at a time. If you mix several and have a reaction, you cannot tell which caused it.
- Stop right away if there is a rash or any bad effect.
- No improvement after two or three doses? See a doctor.
- Boil in a clay or enamel pot, never aluminum. Wash and chop the plant first.
- Avoid plants that were sprayed with insecticide.

## What the nurse does
Make sure it is the right plant, teach the right preparation, and say when to stop and when to see a doctor.

## Common trap
Continuing despite a reaction is always wrong. Herbs do not replace care for serious illness.

## Check against your textbook
Only the plants on the official DOH list are endorsed. Verify the list.
np1-stop-smoking:
## The big idea
Smoking is a leading preventable cause of heart disease, lung disease and cancer. Helping someone quit works best when you match your help to how ready they are, like pushing a swing at the right moment.

## In plain words
- **The 5 A's:** Ask, Advise, Assess willingness, Assist, Arrange follow-up.
- **Stages of change:**
  - Not thinking about quitting: give personal information.
  - Thinking about it: help weigh pros and cons.
  - Planning soon: help set a quit date.
  - Recently quit: support them.
  - Staying quit: prevent relapse.
- Cravings, irritability and poor concentration are normal and fade.
- Relapse is part of the process, not failure.
- Secondhand smoke harms children and pregnant women.

## What the nurse does
Ask about tobacco at every contact. If there is chest pain or breathlessness, treat that first and counsel later.

## Common trap
Do not lecture quit steps to someone who is not ready.

## Check against your textbook
Laws and available medicines change. Verify local details.
np1-g-herbal-plants:
## The big idea
Ten plants are endorsed for community use. The job is to match each plant to its main use. Pair each plant with one symptom or body area.

## In plain words
- **Lagundi:** cough and asthma.
- **Yerba buena:** body pain.
- **Sambong:** swelling and urinary stones.
- **Tsaang gubat:** stomachache.
- **Niyog-niyogan:** roundworm.
- **Bayabas (guava):** cleaning wounds and mouth problems.
- **Akapulko:** skin infections and scabies.
- **Ulasimang bato:** lowers uric acid, for gout.
- **Bawang (garlic):** lowers cholesterol.
- **Ampalaya:** lowers blood sugar in mild diabetes.

## How to prepare
Most leaves are boiled and then drunk in parts through the day. Follow the official instructions for amounts.

## Check against your textbook
Amounts in the handout are unverified. Check the official list before teaching them.
np1-g-health-emergency-program:
## The big idea
This program gets people and health services ready for disasters before they strike. Like practicing a fire drill, preparation done earlier saves more lives than scrambling during the event.

## In plain words
- **Disaster:** a serious disruption that a society cannot handle with its own resources. It may be natural or man-made.
- **Hazard:** anything that could harm people and their surroundings.
- **First priority:** protect the people at risk. **Second:** protect critical resources and systems.
- Main aim: fewer deaths and illnesses, and prevent disability.
- Abilities must be built before impact, not during.
- Risks include floods, earthquakes, typhoons, chemical accidents, epidemics and violence.

## What the nurse does
People first, then critical resources. Prepare, then respond, then help recovery.

## Common trap
Choosing paperwork over action.

## Check against your textbook
The old law named here has been replaced by a newer disaster law. Verify.
np1-x-nutrition-program:
## The big idea
The national nutrition program aims at better nutrition, better health and more productivity. It uses several tools at the same time, like attacking a problem from many sides.

## In plain words
- Common deficiencies: vitamin A, iron, iodine.
- Tools:
  - **Supplementation:** giving tablets or capsules.
  - **Fortification:** adding nutrients to common foods.
  - Maternal and child health services.
  - Nutrition teaching.
  - Growing food at home, school and community.
  - Food assistance and livelihood help.

## What the nurse does
Find who is deficient or at risk, give supplements on schedule, teach feeding and food growing, and link families to help.

## Common trap
Fortification is not supplementation. One adds nutrients to food, the other gives pills.

## Check against your textbook
Program names and schedules change. Verify.
np1-g-blood-services:
## The big idea
This program promotes blood donation that is free, voluntary and safe, so hospitals have enough blood when it is needed. The idea is donating as a kind act, not for payment.

## In plain words
- Donors must be within a set age range and in good health. Some medical conditions rule a person out, such as diabetes, cancer, heart disease, epilepsy, kidney or liver disease, AIDS and other sexually transmitted infections.
- Whole blood and red cells keep for weeks. Plasma can be frozen for months.
- **After donating:** keep the dressing on for a few hours, expect some bruising, avoid heavy lifting with that arm, eat regular meals and drink more fluids. Avoid smoking for two hours and alcohol for twelve hours.

## Check against your textbook
Exact age, weight, blood pressure and hemoglobin limits vary by blood center. Check the numbers there.
np1-g-botika-barangay:
## The big idea
A Botika ng Barangay is a small community drugstore for faraway places where it is hard to buy medicine. Think of it as a neighborhood shop for essential, affordable medicines.

## In plain words
- Goal: make essential medicines available and affordable, especially in hard-to-reach areas.
- It links the DOH, local governments and barangay health workers.
- To start one you need:
  - a recognized community group or cooperative running it
  - a far-flung or poor barangay
  - money shared by the community and the government
  - a licensed pharmacist supervising
  - trained barangay health workers or volunteers as aides
  - a space for the store

## Easy way to remember
Community runs it, pharmacist watches over it, barangay health workers help.

## Check against your textbook
The handout gave amounts and counts. Verify the current rules.
np1-magna-carta:
## The big idea
The Magna Carta of Public Health Workers is a law that protects and rewards people working in government health service, especially in remote places. It helps keep nurses, midwives and doctors in public service.

## In plain words
- It covers workers in **government** health work. Private hospital nurses are not the target.
- Benefits match a burden: hazard pay for risk of exposure, hardship allowance for remote assignment, longevity pay for long service, and allowances for subsistence and laundry.
- It also protects security of tenure and the right to organize.

## Easy way to match
Exposed to infectious disease: hazard pay. Sent to a far-flung barangay: hardship allowance. Long years in service: longevity pay.

## Common trap
Do not assume every benefit applies to every worker.

## Check against your textbook
Law number, amounts and conditions should be copied from your reviewer or the law itself.
np1-copar-phases:
## The big idea
Community organizing moves in a set order, like building a house: prepare the lot, move in, survey, build the frame, put up walls, then let the family live there alone. The nurse steps back as the community takes over.

## In plain words
1. **Pre-entry:** choose the site, study records, look around. Done before going in.
2. **Entry:** blend in with residents and form a core group.
3. **Community study:** gather data, check it with the community, set priorities.
4. **Organization:** elect officers, form committees, train leaders.
5. **Action:** train community health workers, run and monitor projects.
6. **Sustenance:** write rules, grow new leaders, plan ahead, and the nurse steps back.

## Easy way to remember
Prepare, Enter, Study, Organize, Act, Sustain.

## Common trap
Core group formation is in entry. Election of officers is in organization.

## Check against your textbook
Books group the phases differently. Memorize your school's version.
np1-copar-principles:
## The big idea
In community organizing, the **people** decide and the nurse **helps**. Think of a teacher who guides but lets students do the work, so they can still do it after she leaves.

## In plain words
- **The nurse's role:** catalyst, helper and teacher, not the owner of the project.
- Start with small, local problems the people name themselves.
- Action and research happen together. The community collects and studies its own information.
- Leaders emerge through action. The nurse does not appoint them.
- Building the community's ability matters more than any single project.
- The goal is a self-reliant community.

## How to choose answers
Choose the option that returns decisions to the community. Words like facilitator, empowerment and participation point to the right answer.

## Easy way to remember
People decide, nurse facilitates, project survives without her.

## Check against your textbook
Books list five to seven principles in different words. The logic is the same.
np1-g-copar-activities-par:
## The big idea
Besides the six phases, community organizing uses ten repeating activities. It also uses research that the community itself carries out.

## In plain words
Ten activities, in simple terms:
- **Integration:** live with the people to build trust.
- **Social investigation:** study the community's structures and groups.
- **Planning:** choose the actions.
- **Ground work:** one-to-one motivation.
- **Community meeting:** the group agrees on decisions.
- **Role play:** practice the meeting.
- **Mobilization:** people act to solve their problems.
- **Evaluation** and **reflection:** look back at what happened.
- **Organization:** widen participation.

## Participatory action research
The people being helped are the main actors. Community members define the problems and form their own recommendations, with outside researchers working alongside.

## Easy way to compare
Traditional research: experts decide. Participatory research: the community decides.

## Check against your textbook
Books may name or group the activities differently.
np1-mental-health-program:
## The big idea
The community mental health program brings basic mental health care close to home, without shame. Treat mental health as part of overall health, like checking blood pressure.

## In plain words
- Services sit inside primary care. Severe or complex cases are referred.
- Warning signs of risk: talking about wanting to die, giving things away, hopelessness, withdrawing, sudden changes in behavior. Risk is higher with a specific plan, a way to do it and a past attempt.
- **Psychological first aid:** look, listen, link. Check safety, listen without forcing, connect to help.
- Rehabilitation of a recovering client is tertiary prevention.

## What the nurse does
Safety first. If someone may harm themselves, stay with them and get urgent help. Ask directly about suicidal thoughts. Listen without judgment, then refer.

## Common traps
Never leave a suicidal person alone, and never promise to keep a suicide plan secret.

## Check against your textbook
Program names, law numbers and hotlines should be verified locally.
np1-bemoc-cemoc:
## The big idea
Emergency care for mothers and newborns has two levels. Basic (BEmOC) is what a good health center can do. Comprehensive (CEmOC) is basic plus surgery and blood transfusion at a hospital.

## In plain words
- **Basic services:** antibiotics, a medicine that makes the womb contract, magnesium sulfate for convulsions, removing a stuck placenta, removing retained tissue, assisted delivery with vacuum or forceps, newborn resuscitation.
- **Comprehensive adds:** cesarean section and blood transfusion.
- Match the danger to the service: bleeding, convulsions, infection, obstructed labor, baby not breathing.
- **Three delays:** deciding to seek care, reaching the facility, getting care once there.

## Easy way to remember
CEmOC = BEmOC + Cut (cesarean) + Blood.

## What the nurse does
Spot the emergency early, stabilize within your scope, refer with a clear message and an escort, and tell the receiving facility.

## Check against your textbook
The signal function list, and whether newborn resuscitation counts as basic, vary.
